title: Frachetta
html:
Girolamo Frachetta (1558 - 1619). Frachetta wrote about government and war and worked in Roman patronage and information networks. He became Mayenne's informer and managed French postal business in Rome.

In his letter, Desportes addresses Frachetta with some familiarity, apparently trusting him. Frachetta betrayed this trust in September 1593 by providing copies of Desportes' correspondence to the Spanish ambassador.
body:
[Girolamo Frachetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girolamo_Frachetta) (1558 - 1619).  Frachetta wrote about government and war and worked in Roman patronage and information networks.  He became [Mayenne's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Mayenne) informer and managed French postal business in Rome.  

In his letter, Desportes addresses Frachetta with some familiarity, apparently trusting him.  Frachetta betrayed this trust in September 1593 by [providing copies of Desportes' correspondence to the Spanish ambassador](https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/girolamo-frachetta_(Dizionario-Biografico)/).

title: backed by our Doctor Gratian
html:
This reference is almost certainly to the legate, Filippo Sega, who backed various candidates for the Infanta's hand proposed by Philip II of Spain.

"Doctor Gratian" likely refers to Il Dottore, the pompous learned fool of Italian commedia dell'arte. There is a print likely from Paris in the mid-1580s that labels this character "Doctor Gratian".
body:
This reference is almost certainly to the legate, [Filippo Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filippo_Sega), who backed various candidates for the Infanta's hand proposed by [Philip II of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Spain).

"Doctor Gratian" likely refers to *Il Dottore*, the pompous learned fool of Italian commedia dell'arte.  There is [a print likely from Paris in the mid-1580s](https://english.rutgers.edu/images/documents/faculty/buckley_eloquent.pdf#page=57) that labels this character "Doctor Gratian".

title: As for your pension, it cannot be arranged, since no one contributes to it except the prelate to whom the item of revenue is assigned, and this is no time to take anything from him
titleHtml: As for your pension, it cannot be arranged, since no one contributes to it except the prelate to whom the item of revenue is assigned, and this is no time to take anything from him
html:
Desportes apparently refuses Frachetta's requests for additional funds, under the pretext that these funds would have to be obtained from some third party (a prelate), and "this is no time" to ask for funds from that prelate. Desportes also later implies that he has likewise not been paid: "This has been your misfortune and mine."

Just two months after Desportes' letters were written, Frachetta turned over Desportes' correspondence to the Spanish ambassador. One wonders whether Mayenne's refusal to send payment to Frachetta played a role in this decision.

title: the journey of [Gondi]
html: The character reserved for the man who undertook the journey has not been deciphered, but the man is likely Jérôme Gondi, a financier and French royal courtier from the Florentine Gondi family. Gondi conducted diplomatic missions and served as an intermediary between Henry IV and Ferdinando I de’ Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany. Medici, in turn, was the intermediary through whom negotiations were conducted between Henry IV and the Catholic League. It is Gondi who delivered to Medici the April 26, 1593 correspondence from Henry IV in which Henry IV promised to convert to Catholicism.
body: The character reserved for the man who undertook the journey has not been deciphered, but the man is likely Jérôme Gondi, a financier and French royal courtier from the Florentine Gondi family.  Gondi conducted diplomatic missions and served as an intermediary between Henry IV and Ferdinando I de’ Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany.  Medici, in turn, was the intermediary through whom negotiations were conducted between Henry IV and the Catholic League.  It is Gondi who delivered to Medici [the April 26, 1593 correspondence from Henry IV in which Henry IV promised to convert to Catholicism](https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Henri_IV_-_Lettres_Missives_-_Tome3.djvu/792).

title: the withdrawal of five hundred thousand écus
titleHtml: the withdrawal of five hundred thousand écus
html:
In previously known correspondence, Henry IV agreed to convert to Catholicism in exchange for: (1) payment for 4,000 of Henry IV's Swiss troops for one year, (2) payment for 1,000 of additional Swiss troops for six months, and (3) additional payment of 200,000 écus. Desportes' letter reveals the total sum paid to Henry IV for his conversion: 500,000 écus.

This sum (the equivalent of 1,500,000 livres), was a very large payment at the time. In comparison, the payment that Henry IV had to make for finally securing Paris in 1594 was only slightly larger: 1,645,400 livres.
body:
In [previously known correspondence](https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Henri_IV_-_Lettres_Missives_-_Tome3.djvu/793), Henry IV agreed to convert to Catholicism in exchange for: (1) payment for 4,000 of Henry IV's Swiss troops for one year, (2) payment for 1,000 of additional Swiss troops for six months, and (3) additional payment of 200,000 écus.  Desportes' letter reveals the total sum paid to Henry IV for his conversion: 500,000 écus.

This sum (the equivalent of [1,500,000 livres](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.7208/chicago/9780226817583-004/pdf)), was a very large payment at the time.  In comparison, the payment that Henry IV had to make for finally securing Paris in 1594 was only slightly larger: [1,645,400 livres](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/11955/11955-h/11955-h.htm).

title: even failing to have a single one of our briefs delivered
titleHtml: even failing to have a single one of our briefs delivered
html: In the letter to Pietro Aldobrandini, Desportes asks to establish a direct line of communication between Pope Clement VIII and Mayenne. It seems that one reason for this request is that Mayenne's previous correspondence, which he had to forward to Clement VIII through Filippo Sega, was never delivered by the legate.
